replying_to: Replying to GSD: Generalized Stochastic Decoding
display_title: Official Review of Paper4645 by Reviewer eAC1

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduces the generalized stochastic decoding (GSD) framework and the subsequent Intrinsic Decoding algorithm. They formally show how several existing stochastic decoding algorithms can be viewed as special cases of GSD. Further they perform empirical comparison of sequence completions between their Intrinsic Decoding and other algorithms paired with GPT-2 using automatic metrics. They suggest that the GSD can be seen as a platform for future research around stochastic based decoding strategies.
content.main_review:
Here I will concentrate on the weaknesses as I believe they outweigh all strong points which exist too.

1. Important related work is ignored. This paper discusses both generalization of stochastic decoding strategies and a new 'hyper-parameter free algorithm'. Both of these directions have been investigated here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.07243.pdf, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.14966.pdf. This observation alone weakens the strong points of this work as I believe authors indeed may have been unaware of this existing work. This work may be significantly improved if detailed comparison with existing work would be provided. Frankly speaking, I was surprised to see that this paper does not have related work section / paragraph.

2. The evaluation setup does not look strong enough in order to make claims about the efficiency of Intrinsic Decoding. First, no human evaluation was done. As you can see in my detailed feedback part, authors had *many* statements about 'how humans communicate' etc. but they have not done any evaluation involving human judgement. In addition to this, existing algorithms like Mirostat which controls the uncertainty of token-level distribution need to be included in the experiments. Second, authors checked only one single model in one task which was sequence completion. There are many other options which have well settled automatic metrics: machine translation, question answering and so on.

The strong point of this work is the GSD framework itself. I believe authors are able to create better-motivated task conditioned algorithms based on it. Unfortunately, the framework itself can not be directly applied to any specific task / goal so more efforts are certainly required there.

Below I provide more detailed feedback about specific parts of the paper, I hope it can be helpful to authors in order to refine this work.

page 1, "Neither diversity nor fluency is a pre-specified": If we go in this area, then I could imagine a person to condition the style based on the listener at least on the level of vocabulary and diversity.

page 2, "we rarely ask God to configure us with a hyperparameter before uttering individual words.": It is not clear what is the purpose of this statement. When it comes to the hyper-parameters of the decoding algorithms -- they are introduced as constraints on the sequence/token-level distribution of the model.

page 3, "Thus, it has been widely used in many generation tasks until now.": As far as I know, greedy decoding as choice of the final decoding strategy is not used as much beyond low uncertainty tasks e.g. grammar error correction. Provide references to make this statement strong.

page 3, "Theoretically, only when its search width hyper parameter w is equal to the size of the dictionary can it be ensured that the paths sought by Beam Search include the globally optimized solution.": This looks wrong: beam size converging to infinity would correspond to the global exhaustive search.

page 3, "Empirical results in previous works (Welleck et al., 2020) have shown that text generated by Beam Search is prone to text degradation.": I believe the major argument from this work was about the issue of modeling error which may lead to degeneracy with beam search. That is why in the end they showed how better modeling improves beam search predictions in terms of repetitions.

page 3, "both Greedy Decoding and Beam Search are under the same paradigm": Afaik sometimes it is called approximation of the MAP decoding.

page 3, "probabilities assigned by Greedy Decoding and Beam Search are pretty different from the distributions of human language": Example with one specific sentence doesn't help, but may be deceptive. Is there a way to quantify such 'trivial peaks' on the corpus level? I guess what you meant is not 'the distribution of human language', but 'from model probabilities of the samples obtained from data distribution'? 

page 3, "it seems deterministic strategy may not be the best answer to the question of how to get x": Why? It only shows a single example without any details on how the model was trained and so on. Perhaps it is possible to support such statement with more details.

page 4, "Given these observations of how humans communicate": I believe one of main reasons behind truncated sampling based algorithm was to suggest an interpolation between MAP based algorithm and the ancestral sampling. ''How humans communicate' and so on does not sound as verifiable statements. This sounds specifically speculative here given that this work does not do any human-involved evaluation.

page 5, "A benefit of defining ∆ in such a way": about eq5: should delta/k be part of the \phi arguments since it is used as part of the definition? In addition, what is the value of numerator if x is not in delta? Usually in top-k it is 0, this definition would leave it as is.

page 5, "Now, it seems that all problems have been settled.": What problems? Such statements do not help me to understand what problems are solved.

page 5, "Except for Sampling Decoding and Greedy Search,": Greedy search is a special case of beam search so it has the same hyper-parameter. Ancestral sampling (as you write it sampling) is indeed different because it provides unbiased sample from the underlying *sequence-level* distribution defined by the generator.

page 5, "we first propose a more generalized decoding framework referred to as GSD": Were you aware about this work? https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.07243.pdf. They study properties of existing sampling algorithm and unify them under the common conditions. I believe it is not only worth citing, but more importantly comparing with it.

page 7, "While different from all the other methods, Intrinsic Decoding is hyperparameter-free.": Were you aware about Mirostat algorithm (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.14966.pdf)? They use similar uncertainty based computation at each step to compute k for top k sampling. It reminds me a lot your intrinsic decoding method.

page 7: "By setting up different conditions, our framework provides infinite space for new decoding approaches.": Formally there are always infinitely many ways to construct the decoding algorithm, but the question is why the given algorithm makes sense conditioned on task or performance measure. I believe in your case the choice of tau may deviate the generator towards different properties on sequence level. This should be discussed in detail.This again reminds me the Mirostat paper.

page 9: "To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work developing a unified method to bridge existing decoding algorithms using formal theorems and concrete implementations.": I am afraid this is not true as I mentioned before: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.14966.pdf describes the sampling algorithm based on topk where k is computed based on 'surprisal' (similar to uncertainty in your case), https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.07243.pdf unifies existing sampling algorithms rigorously using specific set of constraints.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the major strong weaknesses of this work I do not recommend to accept it in the current state. Nonetheless, I believe authors did decent work assuming they were not aware about multiple highly relevant existing work. I think following major parts are missing in this work which makes it hard be accepted: (1) detailed comparison with existing work, (2) experimental setup checking multiple tasks and targeting specific research questions.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to R4
content.comment:
### Reference Number A4
Thanks a lot for the insightful suggestions for our paper. We are glad that you appreciate the strong points of our proposed decoding framework.

### Reference Number A4_1
First, thank you for the kind reminder. We have carefully read the articles [1] [2] you mentioned, including the codes they provided.

1. Both articles [1] and [2] are excellent works. We have included detailed discussions in the latest submission to compare between the methods proposed in these two articles and ours. After careful reading, we conclude that,

   - Methods proposed in these articles are entirely different from ours. The only connection between our paper and article [1] is the usage of entropy. However, entropy in our paper works independently with the decoding temperature. In contrast, this is not true for article [1], where entropy has an inseparable relationship with the temperature hyper-parameter. Besides, the main contribution of our paper is the generalized decoding framework, in which entropy is replaceable. While, this is not true for article [1], where entropy is irreplaceable. For article [2], we did not find anything that may have a possible connection with our method because we never claim how to adjust our decoding framework to meet a predetermined perplexity. On the contrary, one of the core contributions of our paper is trying to avoid this.

   - Research motives behind these two articles are also quite different from ours. Specifically, article [1] aims to identify fundamental properties shared among some decoding algorithms and investigate what will happen if meeting or violating the identified properties. For article [2], it aims to design a feedback-based adaptive top-k decoding algorithm that generates text with a predetermined perplexity. None of them aim to design a generalized decoding framework that can be used to describe and connect existing popular decoding algorithms, which is just the focus of our paper.

We agree that we should discuss these two articles because both are relatively new works in this field. However, we disagree that missing discussions about these two articles significantly affect the innovations of our paper. Even for these two articles, they do not make any comparison or discussion with each other, which did not prevent their acceptance and publication.

2. We plan to add experiments to compare our method with the methods proposed in these two articles [1] [2]. However, we got some problems in running the codes provided in these two articles. 

Concretely, article [1] provides a solid code project including almost everything to run and evaluate their method. But we can not launch it because both links to download the datasets and the model files are invalid with 404 responded from the server. (i.e., http://moinnadeem.com/csa/models.zip and http://moinnadeem.com/csa/gigaword_data.zip). While for article [2], there is only one Python file illustrating how their method works. It does not support basic batch operations, let alone any instructions to conduct evaluations. Therefore, we are unable to compare it using the same dataset in our article. 

Thank you for the kind remainder. We have added a detailed comparison to [1] and [2] in the related work section. Although we cannot run comparisons using the codes provided by [1] and [2], we have begun to write new implementations based on the method descriptions presented in their articles. It takes time to finish. Results will be added to the camera-ready submission.

### Reference Number A4_2
Second, thanks a lot for your feedback. Following your suggestions, we have renamed the second subsection by related work and added more discussions about relatively new works in this field. Please also refer to **A0_3** for details.

### Reference Number A4_3
Third, about human evaluations, please refer to **A1_3** for details.

### Reference Number A4_4
Fourth, GPT-2 is a popular generator that has been widely used by many previous works [1], [2], [3] [4], including Top-p [3] and your mentioned two articles [1], [2]. Especially for your mentioned article [1] and the article proposing the popular Top-p decoding algorithm [3], GPT-2 is the only generator that has been considered just as our paper. More importantly, for both articles [1] [2] mentioned by you, the open-ended language generation task is the only task that has been used to evaluate their methods, same as our paper.

### Reference Number A4_5
We have eliminated all the problems about the details of our paper. But due to the limit of 5000 words, we can't list these revisions here. Thanks a lot for the kind reviews, which make our work more polished.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper deals with decoding algorithms for neural text generation. The paper proposes a way to connect greedy decoding, beam search, (ancestral) sampling, top-k sampling, top-p (nucleus) sampling. The proposed GSD is on page 6 (specifically, equations 8, 9, 10). The visualization for how equations 8-10 tie the decoding algorithms together is in Figure 1. The authors claim that this generalization can provide an “infinite space” for designing more decoding algorithms. Empirical results show that open-domain text generation from GPT-2 using GSD results in a perplexity that’s closer to the human perplexity, and a self-BLEU that’s closer to the human self-BLEU.
content.main_review:
I need to acknowledge that Equations 8-10 which tie the decoding algorithms are clever. Yes, using different $\tau$ in GSD might give us more decoding algorithms. 

The background introduction (although long) is great, so that readers who don’t have an in-depth knowledge in text generation decoding algorithms will be on the same page. 

It’s not clear why we need a hyperparameter-free decoding algorithm (and even if the authors' motivation convince us to use hyperparemter-free decoding algorithm, related works are not mentioned). Moreover, the authors show that the perplexity for generated texts is close to the human perplexity. But we can manipulate the temperature in ancestral sampling, top-k, top-p, or the k in top-k, the p in top-p, or we can even create some hand-crafted decoding algorithm on our own to generate a perplexity that’s close to human texts’. This doesn’t mean that the decoded texts are “high-quality.”

On page 4, the motivation is that “everyone has a preferred way to speak and has a unique subset dictionary to realize this personalization” but this is not necessarily true in all text generation tasks. We want diversity in some tasks (dialogue, open-domain text generation) but for some other tasks like machine translation, summarization, and table-to-text summarization, one good output is enough. Related work for “generating one good output is enough”: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=RovX-uQ1Hua. So it’s not clear if GSD will be useful in those tasks. 

Relatively minor:
- On page 5, the definitions of top-p decoding could be incorrect in certain corner cases. For example, let p=0.1, and suppose the token probabilities for the top 6 tokens are 0.15, 0.14, 0.13, 0.12, 0.11, 0.10. The authors’ definition allows us to choose any of the 6 words, but we should instead choose the top-probability token. To be fair, this scenario probably doesn’t appear too often in practice. 

The writing could be more precise and clearer. For example…
- In the abstract, “why text generated from these algorithms are divergent” -- it’s unclear what “divergent” means.
- In the abstract, “novel implementation with a distinctive core” -- unclear what “core” means.
- On page 2, section 2.1, what’s $\delta$? It’ll be great if the authors can immediately explain what this new symbol refers to after mentioning it. 
- For Figure 2, it’s not clear what the context is. Is it a cherry-picked example? Is there ever <eos>? More explanations of what’s going on will be great. 
- In Eq. (2), it’ll be best if the authors can immediately describe what kind of object $\phi$ is. 
- In Eq. (8), it’s helpful to write what’s under the summation sign, and expand P, given that it’s the few most important equations in the entire paper. 
- On page 8, do you mean Figure 3 instead of Figure 4.2?

Slightly confusing: on top of page 2, the authors say “we rarely ask God to configure us with a hyperparameter before uttering individual words.” But then the authors also claim that “everyone has a preferred way to speak” and “it usually depends on personal habits of language use.” So this sounds like a hyperparameter to me? Why do we need a hyperparameter-free decoding algorithm?

The logic on page 3, in the “another deterministic decoding algorithm is beam search” paragraph is a bit incorrect in my opinion. The authors claim that given that we cannot find the optimal path (i.e., search error), beam search leads to degenerations. But the issue might be modeling errors as well. For example, see Murray and Chiang (2018): https://aclanthology.org/W18-6322.pdf, and a more recent paper: https://aclanthology.org/D19-1331/. Beam search with very large beam size could generate empty translations. As an aside, Welleck et al. (EMNLP 2020), Consistency of a Recurrent Language Model With Respect to Incomplete Decoding, is also a related paper addressing the repetition issue; it shows that greedy, beam search, top-k, top-p can all generate repetitions and proposed decoding algorithms to avoid the repetition issue.

Relatively minor:
- Page 1, line 4-5 of the introduction, the authors forgot to mention nucleus/top-p sampling before citing the paper
- When the authors are citing multiple papers consecutively, it’s best to do (xx et al.; yy et al.; zz et al.) instead of  (xx et al.) (yy et al.) (zz et al.)
content.summary_of_the_review: Equations 8-10 which tie the decoding algorithms together are clever. However, it's not clear why we need a parameter-free decoding algorithm from the authors' discussion (and to be fair, $\tau$ is still like a parameter), and it's not clear how more algorithms created from GSD are useful/good. The result that we can generate texts with a similar perplexity as humans' does not prove that the generations are "high-quality" and can be adapted to other tasks.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

Thank you for the insightful comments and feedback, which are very important to help improve the quality of our paper. We have made corresponding revisions to respond to these comments, including clarifications of some misunderstandings.

### Reference Number A3_1
First, thank you very much for appreciating the detailed introductions of existing algorithms. Also, we have revised Section 2 to compact some verbose introductions and added discussions of some new articles in this field.

Thanks a lot for helping us improve the reading experience of Section 2.

### Reference Number A3_2
Second, we have revised the paper to clarify why we need a hyper-parameter-free decoding algorithm, for example, the last two paragraphs of section 2.2.

### Reference Number A3_3
Third, we agree that one can manipulate the temperature in ancestral sampling, top-k, top-p, or the k in top-k, the p in top-p. However, all these approaches are not practical for the following reasons:

1. Assuming we have found a proper hyper-parameter in brute-force after trying different k, p, or temperatures, and finally got excellent consecutive generations closing to human texts. Then, the second context in the same batch comes. Is it true that the previous proper hyper-parameter still works for this different context? 

2. One of the most important goals of machine learning and artificial intelligence is to help human beings make valuable decisions. We disagree that manipulating these hyper-parameters in a hand-crafted way aligns with the long-term vision of artificial intelligence. Even in some scenarios, manual selections of these hyper-parameters lead to ideal results. These scenarios cannot cover all artificial intelligence tasks. Isn’t this the value of us AI researchers?

Thanks a lot for the kind comment. It helps a lot to make our work more clear to understand.

### Reference Number A3_4
Fourth, the mentioned article [1] is excellent. It models the generation task as an offline reinforcement learning task with reference demonstrations. We have discussed it in the latest submission as one of the related works.

We fully agree that one good output is enough for some tasks like machine translation, summarization, and table-to-text summarization. However, it is not always enough to generate only one sound output. Moreover, the reason has already been explained by you: we want diversity in some other tasks (dialogue, open-domain text generation).

Thanks for the mentioned article, which helps a lot to highlight our contributions.

### Reference Number A3_5
Fifth, given your example, let p=0.1, and suppose the token probabilities for the top 6 tokens are 0.15, 0.14, 0.13, 0.12, 0.11, 0.10. The definition allows us to choose from these six words, which is just how nucleus sampling (Top-p) works. We don't understand why we should instead choose the top-probability token? Do you mean Top-k decoding? 

### Reference Number A3_6
Minor revisions:

- In the abstract, “why text generated from these algorithms are divergent ?” has been revised to “why text generated from these algorithms are degenerated ?”

- In the abstract, “novel implementation with a distinctive core” has been revised to “a novel implementation with distinctive design.”

- On page 2, section 2.1, we have added explanations about what $\delta$ means. Actually, it represents a span containing the context.

- In Equation (2), as explained in the third paragraph of section 2.2, $\phi$ is a function to represent the relationship between $P(x | \mathbf{x}_\delta)$ and $\widehat{P} (x | \mathbf{x}_\delta)$.

- On page 8, yes, we do mean Figure 3 instead of Figure 4.2. This is a bug in the latex sub-figure command. We have updated the location where the label of Figure 3 was inserted. It is correctly displayed now. Thanks a lot for the insightful remainder.

- On top of page 2, we have re-organized the expressions in this paragraph.

- On page 3, we have re-organized the third paragraph. Thanks for the kind reminder. We have carefully read the mentioned articles [2] [3] [4] and agree with your opinion that increasing $w$ will not always lead to better generations. Also, we have added discussions to these articles in our related work section to highlight this conclusion.
Besides, re-organizing these paragraphs about related works does not affect the contributions of our paper.

- Thanks for helping check the citation styles. We have proofread them and revised the consecutive citations in the format as suggested. Now, these citations look much cleaner than in the previous submission.

Thanks a lot for these comments, which are essential to help improve the quality of our paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper concerns decoding from language models. The authors give a formulation that contains several decoding as special cases, and a sampling algorithm which uses entropy averaged over a batch of sequences.
content.main_review:
**Clarity**. The paper's clarity is below the bar for ICLR. It contains many:
- Unsubstantiated claims (e.g. "virtually all decoding methods currently developed are pragmatic to address the text degeneration problem").
- Verbose presentations (e.g. sections 2.1 and 2.2 take up 3 pages but don't introduce anything new).
- Hand-wavy, imprecise explanations (e.g. "In communications, people prefer to sample words from this subset rather than searching from the whole dictionary. This personalized sub-vocabulary is essential to make up distinct oral and writing styles of human communications").

If needed, I can provide more examples.

**Theoretical significance of method**. While it is indeed possible to view existing algorithms as special cases of equations (8-10),  we do not get much insight from doing so (or at least the paper has not articulated these insights). This aspect is important since there are many possible generalized equations that yield existing algorithms as special cases, so we need to know why this one is notable.

**Method**. The use of entropy is not well-motivated by the authors (and this choice impacts the resulting formulation). The statement "we prefer to use entropy since variance is relatively harder to control because of its unlimited value range" does not provide enough justification. Second, the dependence on the contents of the batch and the batch size is puzzling (equation 15). Does the proposed method not work with batch size 1? How does the sampling change as the properties of the batch change (e.g. a batch of "similar" sequences versus "different" sequences)?

**Experimental quality and empirical analysis**. The empirical analysis and experimental quality are below the bar for ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the idea of a generalized stochastic decoding algorithm that does not require hyperparameters is interesting, the presentation, contributions, and empirical analysis in this paper would need substantial improvements for me to argue for acceptance.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4645 by Reviewer fbQi

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a fairly general approach to generating from language models: words are sampled from a renormalized distribution consisting of the smallest set of words in the vocabulary which together have probability at least $\rho$, where $\rho$ is a function of the entropy of the distribution. The authors show that several standard decoding algorithms arise from particular choices of $\rho$. The authors then propose to use a particular $\rho$, essentially $\tanh(\text{entropy}/\text{average batch entropy})$, which they argue is attractive because it has no hyperparameters. The authors evaluate the generations obtained from decoding with their approach by comparing them to baseline generations in terms of perplexity assigned to generations by GPT-2, self-BLEU, and other recent automatic metrics.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The paper is an engaging read.
- The core idea of being more conservative when the entropy of the word distribution is low and less otherwise seems reasonable.

Weaknesses:
- It's rather strange to have a decoding algorithm depend on the batch and batch size. (Indeed, this is especially strange given the authors' emphasis on constructing a human-like decoding algorithm, and on not having any hyperparameters).
- The experimental procedure and results are rather unclear. First, despite the decoding algorithm depending on the batch, I don't think the authors mention what batch size they use, or what the results look like for different batch sizes. It's also unclear how the authors chose which  results should go in Table 1. In particular, although the authors apparently tried using p=0.9 for nucleus sampling (Section 4.1) these results are not in the table. Furthermore, the authors appear to neither try nor report the results for the best setting of p in nucleus sampling (p=0.95)  according to the original paper (Holtzmann et al., 2020).
- The paper is missing a human evaluation of generation quality, which did, for instance, appear in the Holtzmann et al. paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an interesting idea, but the experimental evaluation is incomplete and not well described.

Thanks a lot for the insightful reviews. We are glad to know that you notice our idea is interesting and the paper is engaging. We also appreciate your efforts to help us find deficiencies in our work. Careful revisions have been made to mitigate all these deficiencies. 

### Reference Number A1_1
First, the default batch size used for all generations is 50. Thank you for the kind reminder. We have added a description for the batch configuration in the latest revision. We use $|B|$ in formula (15) to conduct average because,

1. $\gamma$ in formula (15) is a vector with shape (batch size, 1). It must be averaged to a scalar before going to the next step to construct the sampling distribution. To this end, dividing by the batch size $|B|$ is the standard operation for averaging elements in a vector.

2. Since decoding algorithms aim to produce subsequent text based on the given context, each batch is the only source containing all the contexts for decoding. From this point of view, it is reasonable to include batch information in the formula (15).

3. Our decoding method works well even if the batch size is 1. 

To support our claims, we have conducted a lot of additional experiments. Here are the results under different batch sizes:

| Batch Size | PPL       | Self-BLEU | Zipf     | Distinct Rate |
|  ----      |    ----   |  ----     |  ----    |  ----         |
| 1          |  9.763410 | 0.359753  | 0.917093 | 0.590382      |
| 10         | 13.396001 | 0.321623  | 1.008585 | 0.623370      |
| 20         | 12.434328 | 0.310692  | 0.967500 | 0.648903      |
| 30         | 14.861717 | 0.272548  | 0.917186 | 0.664635      |
| 40         | 14.722827 | 0.305332  | 0.911343 | 0.659238      |
| 50         | 13.781747 | 0.350221  | 0.906322 | 0.632566      |

From this table, we can not draw any meaningful conclusion related to the batch size. Formally, according to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), the mean of the samples will approach the mean of the population with infinite precision if the number of samples increases to infinite. Therefore, the only effect of increasing the batch size is making formula (15) closer to the mean of population entropy.

Also, it can be verified from this table that changing the batch size not only does not hinder the performance of our method, but in some cases it gives better results than using the default batch size 50. But we do not intend to report these better results because the core innovation of our paper is to propose a generalized decoding framework. In this framework, not only can existing popular decoding methods be considered as special cases, but also more decoding algorithms can be designed. 

Thanks a lot for the kind reminder. We have added the missing description of the batch configuration.

### Reference Number A1_2
Second, we have revised the paper to include the result of p=0.95 for nucleus sampling. In fact, the entry of p=0.95 for nucleus sampling has already been included in the right part of Figure 3. We have copied the value from the right part of Figure 3 to Table 1. 

Thank you for the kind review to help improve our experiment reports.

### Reference Number A1_3
Third, for human evaluations, we have already given a lot of human-derived quality information in Table 1, Figure 2, and Figure 4 in the appendix. These human evaluations are derived from authentic human-generated texts in the test set. Meanwhile, we did not publish any human assessments of questionnaires on any crowdsourcing platform. We did not conduct this type of crowdsourced questionnaire evaluation based on the following considerations.

1. There are many drawbacks to publishing the generated text for evaluation on a crowdsourcing platform like Mechanical Turk because the result does not entirely depend on the quality of the text. Almost all crowdsourcing platforms are profit-driven, and the purpose of people participating in crowdsourcing is utilitarian. The result depends to a large extent on the mood of the person participating in the evaluation and the quick completion of the evaluation in order to participate in other evaluations to obtain greater benefits. In other words, we only know the result of the evaluation, but we do not know how it comes.

2. Some works preferring to conduct human evaluations through questionnaire-type crowdsourced tests. This approach may be meaningful, but we insist that human evaluations should be more open. So we put all the text generated by the baselines and our method on GitHub before submitting our article such that they can be better evaluated by all the people around the world. The generated text can be accessed from https://github.com/ginoailab/gsd.git.

Furthermore, we also warmly welcome and suggest that researchers in the community can make more extensive and diverse discussions about what types of human evaluations are reasonable.

Thank you for the valuable comments, which help a lot to polish our paper.

content.title: Thanks for your response
content.comment: Thank you for your response. I disagree with the authors' view that having a decoding algorithm depend on the batch size is reasonable. It also looks to me like the batch size does matter (e.g., for a batch of size 1 it looks like the proposed method does not outperform baselines in terms of ppl). More importantly, while I agree with the authors that there are issues with human evaluation, I don't think we have enough evidence of the value of the proposed approach from just Table 1 (and direct human evaluation could conceivably have helped to address this).

content.title: Thanks a lot for the comments.
content.comment:
First, we have conducted a lot of additional experiments and given detailed explanations to respond to your reviews. Please help us to understand why a decoding algorithm should not depend on batch. It will be better if formal mathematical proofs and experiments are available to support this point of view. A decoding algorithm generates text based on input context, and all the context is included in the batch. We are perplexed why the decoding algorithm should not have any relationship with the batch. For example, a function F receives a parameter x and outputs y = F(x). The question is, why F should not be related to x? If the assumption holds, then all existing algorithms should not receive any input and give output directly. Does it make sense?

Second, we have clearly described the default configuration of the batch size in our paper, which is 50. According to the law of Central Limit Theorem (CLT), the larger the number of samples, the more accurately the mean of samples will approximate the population's mean. Thus, we used a relatively large batch size as the default configuration instead of 1. That is, we did not use batch size = 1 in our paper. Is there any problem? Even under batch size = 1 that we did not use in our paper, the mentioned PPL is still better than most (60%) baselines. So, it makes us very confused why "for a batch of size 1, it looks like the proposed method does not outperform baselines in terms of ppl ?"

Third, the core contribution of our paper is to propose a generalized decoding framework that can be used to describe and connect existing popular decoding algorithms. As far as we know, this is the first work trying to propose a generalized framework to bridge these decoding algorithms using formal theorems. Intrinsic Decoding is just an implementation of this framework. It is one of our contributions, but not the core contribution. After rebuttal, the third and fourth reviewers have made a clear understanding of our core contribution. However, we found that this is not true for the concerns expressed, which shocked us.

Finally, we are pleased that you agree with us that there are issues with human evaluation. Thus, besides Table 1, we have uploaded all the generations produced by the baselines and our methods to GitHub (https://github.com/ginoailab/gsd.git) such that all the people around the world can directly evaluate our methods. Also, we must point out that all existing decoding algorithms rely on batch. No matter the batch size is one or other values, it is the input of any decoding algorithm. According to the common sense of computer science, an algorithm or method that does not rely on input and gives output directly is meaningless.

Furthermore, we firmly believe that one critical reason why science is science rather than theology is that science can accommodate different voices. Just as heliocentric theory replaces geocentric theory, the establishment of ICLR is based on such scientific common sense. ICLR has become an attractive place to present technical and empirical novelties in artificial intelligence, rather than a place subordinate to the Pope, who thinks that geocentric theory is the perfect theory in the universe. In this paper, we present a novel decoding framework and use formal mathematical proofs and experiments to verify its effectiveness. We have confidence in our work and hope that the contributions can be accepted by the community.

Thank you very much for your efforts to help us, hoping that the clarifications and answers can help us reach a consensus.

content.title: To All Reviewers
content.comment:
### Reference Number A0
Dear Reviewers,

Thank you very much for taking the time to review our paper. Some of the most important questions and our answers are listed below. Please refer to responses after each reviewer’s comments for details.

### Reference Number A0_1
1. There are two articles [1] [2] that we didn't notice before we started our work. After carefully reading these articles, we found that they did not affect the innovations of our paper at all. Because

    - Methods proposed in these articles are entirely different from ours. The only connection between our paper and article [1] is the usage of entropy. However, entropy in our paper works independently with the decoding temperature. In contrast, this is not true for article [1], where entropy has an inseparable relationship with the temperature hyper-parameter. Besides, the main contribution of our paper is the generalized decoding framework, in which entropy is replaceable. While, this is not true for article [1], where entropy is irreplaceable. For article [2], we did not find anything that may have a possible connection with our method because we never claim how to adjust our decoding framework to meet a predetermined perplexity. On the contrary, one of the core contributions of our paper is trying to avoid this. 

    - Research motives behind these two articles are also quite different from ours. Specifically, article [1] aims to identify fundamental properties shared among some decoding algorithms and investigate what will happen if meeting or violating the identified properties. For article [2], it aims to design a feedback-based adaptive top-k decoding algorithm that generates text with a predetermined perplexity. None of them aim to design a generalized decoding framework that can be used to describe and connect existing popular decoding algorithms, which is just the focus of our paper.

Please refer to **A4_1** for details.

### Reference Number A0_2
2. Two reviewers expressed their concerns about why one of our proposed methods (i.e., Intrinsic Decoding) has a connection with the batch. As we will explain in **A1_1**, this is reasonable because,

    - $\gamma$ in Equation (15) is a vector with shape (batch size, 1). A standard average operation is needed to measure the overall trend of entropy in the current batch. Dividing by $|B|$ is the standard operation for averaging.

    - It is not surprising at all that the decoding algorithm relies on the batch. On the contrary, it seems more strange that a decoding algorithm does not rely on batch. The decoding algorithm aims to produce generations based on given contexts, while all contexts are contained in batches. Why is it surprising that the decoding algorithm depends on batch? Isn't that natural? 

To support our claims, we have conducted a lot of additional experiments. Please refer to **A1_1** for the table containing results under different batch sizes. It can be verified from this table that changing the batch size not only does not hinder the performance of our method, but in some cases it gives better results than using the default batch size 50. 

Please refer to **A1_1** and **A2_5** for details.

### Reference Number A0_3
3. Three reviewers gave comments on the background/related work section of our paper. Specifically, the second reviewer feels that the background/related work section is verbose. While the third reviewer said that the background/related work is excellent so that readers who do not have in-depth knowledge in text generation decoding algorithms will be on the same page. Finally, the last reviewer commented that he/she was surprised to see that this paper does not have a related work paragraph. Based on this embarrassing situation, we must make a unified reply here:

  - We have revised the title of section 2.2 to “related work” to keep consistent with the habits of other articles. Also, we have included more discussions about some latest works in this field.

  - In fact, we can use simplified paragraphs to describe these related works in section 2. However, this has two disadvantages. One is that it is not conducive for researchers from other fields to clearly understand our work, just as the third reviewer said. The other disadvantage is that it will be harder to verify our contributions and the differences between our methods and these related works.

Following the comments, we have made a lot of streamlining for Section 2. Please refer to **A2_2**, **A3_1** and **A4_2** for details.

Finally, what we want to say most is: sincerely thanks for the efforts to help us! We have attached great importance to each feedback and hold many meetings to carefully discuss them, hoping that the clarifications and answers can help us reach a consensus.


### References

[1] *A Systematic Characterization of Sampling Algorithms for Open-ended Language Generation.*

[2] *Mirostat: A Neural Text Decoding Algorithm that Directly Controls Perplexity.*
